tier_reason: Stays B on the peer-reviewed PPoPP '26 paper (Parallel Dynamic Spatial Indexes, doi 10.1145/3774934.3786412) with public scripts and raw CSV (script/data/real_world/real_world.csv, tests/boost_rtree.cpp, tests/test_framework.h), plus Zd-tree rows in the same harness. Not A: CPU model and the compiler used for the paper runs are not stated. Verdict is downgrade because the record's Boost claim was overstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Ratios derived from page data (real_world.csv 'tot' column, seconds). Read the Boost rows carefully: script/merge_real_world.py maps Boost's '## incre insert full' to Insert/1.0, '## incre insert half' to Insert/0.0001 and '## incre delete half' to Delete/0.0001. So Boost 'Insert 1.0' is n sequential single-point inserts into a quadratic bgi::rtree, and Boost's '0.0001' rows are n/2 single-point inserts or deletes. PSI '1.0' is one parallel batch insert of all n points (a build), and PSI '0.0001' is all n points inserted, or deleted, in 10^4 parallel batches. Whole set: Cosmo50 Boost 414.38 vs P-Orth (OrthTree) 1.899 and SPaC-Z (PTree-Z) 0.8365 (about 218x and 495x); OSM 666.0 vs 4.960 and 2.122 (about 134x and 314x); GeoLife 0.2132 vs 0.00639 and PTree-H 0.00150 (about 33x and 142x). Deletes: Cosmo50 Boost 1482.7 s for n/2 single deletes vs OrthTree 17.85 and PTree-Z 8.463 for all n in batches (about 83x and 175x in total time, with Boost doing half the work); OSM 264.2 vs 14.93 and 7.368 (about 18x and 36x). On GeoLife, Boost's n/2 single deletes take less total time (0.064) than OrthTree (0.089) or PTree-H (0.137) deleting all n. Large range report (RRL), both sides parallel: Cosmo50 Boost 19.25 vs OrthTree 1.738, OSM 8.347 vs 1.128, GeoLife 7.829 vs 0.4466 (about 7-18x). Small range report (RRS) favours Boost: Cosmo50 0.00044 vs OrthTree 0.00082, OSM 0.00026 vs 0.00063, GeoLife 0.00028 vs 0.00086. Boost k-NN columns are not comparable (harness bug, see caveats). Against the third-party parallel Zd-tree in the same harness: SPaC-Z batch updates at 0.01% are about 2.1-3.2x faster (Cosmo50 insert 13.83 vs 5.631, delete 20.66 vs 8.463; OSM insert 16.50 vs 7.906, delete 23.86 vs 7.368), and P-Orth is roughly on par with Zd-tree (0.85-1.6x). The SPaC-Z build is about 2.0-2.8x faster than Zd-tree on Cosmo50 and OSM. On queries, P-Orth beats Zd-tree on large range report (Cosmo50 1.738 vs 2.197) and k=10 uniform k-NN (0.244 vs 0.301), while SPaC trees are much slower on k-NN (Cosmo50 IDU10 PTree-H 1.869, PTree-Z 11.55). Paper (search summary only): P-Orth and SPaC trees beat existing parallel kd-trees and Orth-trees on batch updates, with competitive queries, and SPaC-trees are 2-6x faster than Pkd-trees on updates.
corrections.workload: Real-world point sets GeoLife (3-D), Cosmo50 (3-D) and OSM (2-D): whole-set build, all n points inserted or deleted in 10^4 batches of 0.01%, k-NN (k=1,10,100) on four query distributions, and range count/report (small/medium/large). Parallel PSI trees and the parallel Zd-tree are compared against a Boost bgi::rtree<quadratic<32>> that is updated one point at a time on one thread and queried in parallel with parlay::parallel_for (script/data/real_world/real_world.csv, from the PPoPP '26 scripts).
corrections.hardware: CPU model not stated in the repo; docs/ARTIFACT_EVALUATION.md asks for at least 512 GB RAM and preferably more than 128 cores; run scripts use numactl -i all. A search summary of the paper mentions 72 cores with 2-way hyperthreading (unverified, paper blocked).
corrections.caveats: The Boost baseline harness (tests/boost_rtree.cpp) has three problems. (1) Its k-NN loop (run_rtree_knn) ignores the query set it is given and queries wp[0..batch_size) for all four distributions, building each query point from only pnt[0] and pnt[1], so 3-D data sets (Cosmo50, GeoLife) get a query point whose third coordinate does not come from the data. The Boost k-NN times are therefore nearly identical across the IDS/ODS/IDU/ODU columns (Cosmo50 k=10: 0.2735, 0.2765, 0.2759, 0.2756) and are not comparable with PSI's. (2) Boost updates are sequential single-point insert/remove, while PSI and Zd-tree use parallel batches; Boost's bulk-loading (packing) constructor is timed as '## build tree half' but merge_real_world.py drops it, so the 134-495x 'build' ratios compare a parallel build with Boost's slowest construction path. (3) merge_real_world.py labels Boost's n/2 single-point insert/delete runs as ratio 0.0001, so those rows do half the work of the PSI rows with the same label. Boost queries run in parallel, so the range-query ratios are parallel against parallel; Boost wins small range reports on all three data sets. Numbers come from the paper-era code: the README says the library was later refactored with AI and some indexes are 'slightly affected' (original design at commit af67b82). The paper (dl.acm.org, cs.ucr.edu, conference-publishing.com) was blocked, so peer review is confirmed from the README citation and search results only. Pkd-tree (kd_tree.h, KdTree rows) is part of this library and is catalogued separately as ucrparlay/pkd-tree; on Cosmo50, Pkd-tree's 0.01% batch deletes total 800.3 s vs 8.46 s for SPaC-Z. include/psi/dependence/space_filling_curve/hilbert.hpp is under a Rice University notice license (attribution notice required); the CPAM fork and the submodules are MIT.

notes: Metadata confirmed (MIT, 10 stars, 0 forks, 734 commits, last commit 2026-09-09, not a fork). Shortcomings worth recording: Boost k-NN harness bug (wrong query points), mislabeled Boost update rows, and a 'build' comparison against one-at-a-time insertion rather than Boost's bulk loader. The fair third-party comparison is Zd-tree in the same CSV (SPaC-Z about 2-3x faster on batch updates).

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the peer-reviewed FAST-LIO2 paper (IEEE T-RO 2022; PDF in hku-mars/FAST_LIO doc/Fast_LIO_2.pdf) benchmarks ikd-Tree against the Boost.Geometry R*-tree, PCL octree and nanoflann dynamic k-d tree on 18 sequences (Table III, Fig. 5) on an Intel i7-8550U. Not A: the integration code for the three baselines is not public and no compiler or flags are stated.

corrections.baseline: Boost.Geometry R*-tree, PCL octree and nanoflann dynamic k-d tree, each integrated into FAST-LIO2 (FAST-LIO2, IEEE T-RO 2022, Table III); also a static k-d tree rebuilt every scan (FAST-LIO, and the ikd-Tree preprint's PCL comparison)
corrections.claimed_speedup: FAST-LIO2 Table III (average ms per scan over 18 sequences, single-thread kNN; ratios derived from page data): total time (incremental update + kNN), ikd-Tree vs Boost.Geometry R*-tree 1.26-2.09x faster (e.g. nclt 3: 15.42 vs 32.29 ms; utbm 1: 18.42 vs 26.50), vs PCL octree 2.29-3.06x (utbm 1: 18.42 vs 45.00), vs nanoflann 1.03-1.34x (nclt 1: 15.64 vs 20.41). kNN search: R*-tree 1.25-2.09x slower, nanoflann 1.04-1.34x slower, octree 2.6-3.3x slower. Incremental update: the octree is fastest in most sequences (ikd-Tree up to 1.8x slower, e.g. utbm 1 3.23 vs 2.12 ms); ikd-Tree beats the R*-tree by 1.17-2.2x, and nanoflann is slightly faster on ulhk 1-3 and lili 2. Worst case: nanoflann's incremental-update peaks exceed 3 s on seven utbm sequences and 7 s on three nclt sequences, against an ikd-Tree maximum of 214.4 ms (nclt 2) and under 150 ms elsewhere. System level (Table VII): FAST-LIO, which rebuilds a static k-d tree each scan, spends 13.81 ms per scan on mapping vs 0.13 ms for FAST-LIO2 with ikd-Tree (Intel). The ikd-Tree preprint numbers (about 1.6 ms vs over 10 ms for PCL's static tree; 4% of static computation time) were seen only through search snippets.
corrections.hardware: DJI Manifold 2-C: Intel Core i7-8550U (1.8 GHz, 4 cores), 8 GB RAM, for the data-structure comparison; FAST-LIO2 alone was also run on a Khadas VIM3 (2.2 GHz Cortex-A73, 4 GB RAM).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the FAST-LIO2 paper. The ikd-Tree demo CMakeLists uses -std=c++14 -pthread -O3 and links PCL.
corrections.caveats: The evidence is a peer-reviewed paper by the same group (first-party but reviewed). The baselines were wrapped into FAST-LIO2 by the authors, with downsampling emulated through range or radius search for the R*-tree, octree and nanoflann (nanoflann masks deleted points instead of removing them, so its tree grows); that integration code is not public. ikd-Tree is not uniformly faster: the PCL octree has the fastest incremental updates in most sequences, and nanoflann's updates are slightly faster on ulhk 1-3 and lili 2. The gain over nanoflann in total time is small (3-34%); the main advantage is bounded worst-case latency. The 13.81 vs 0.13 ms mapping figure compares two different SLAM pipelines (FAST-LIO rebuilds a static tree per scan), so it measures incremental vs rebuild, not tree speed. The repo's own demo (examples/ikd_Tree_demo.cpp) times only ikd-Tree. The header includes pcl/point_types.h, so PCL is a dependency. Last commit 2022-03-04. README says GPLv2 (links the GPL-2.0 text) with no 'or later' clause and asks commercial users to contact the authors; SPDX GPL-2.0-only is a reading of that.

tier_reason: The author's own Criterion suite (sdd/kd-tree-comparison benches/*.rs, results in all-benchmarks.json) names the CPU (Ryzen 5900X) but not the rustc version or RUSTFLAGS, and the competitors are Python/Rust libraries, not the category's baselines, so C.

corrections.workload: Nearest-1/10/100, within-radius and construction on 100 to 10M points, 2-4 dimensions, f32/f64, 1,000 query points per Criterion iteration (companion repo sdd/kd-tree-comparison). The bench code generates uniform random points in the unit hypercube (rand::random, np.random.rand), although the Kiddo README says the points lie on a unit sphere.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Derived from page data (all-benchmarks.json, 3-D f64, 1,000,000 points, Criterion mean in ns per 1,000-query iteration): Query Nearest 1: Kiddo_v5_immutable_dynamic 49,798 (Kiddo_v3_immutable 44,366) vs nabo 71,993 (about 1.45x), pykdtree 77,187 (about 1.55x), FNNTW 80,818, scipy 907,836 (about 18x), sklearn 1,911,706 (about 38x). Query Nearest 10: Kiddo_v3_std 109,819 vs nabo 131,085 (about 1.2x), pykdtree 199,638 (about 1.8x), scipy 2,227,477 (about 20x). Query Nearest 100: Kiddo_v5_immutable_dynamic 550,945 vs nabo 677,895 (about 1.2x), pykdtree 1,789,125 (about 3.2x). Construction is not faster: Kiddo_v5_immutable_dynamic 161.4 ms and Kiddo_v3_std 124.6 ms vs pykdtree 92.3 ms (scipy 294.8 ms). The scipy and sklearn ratios compare parallel against single-threaded code (see caveats).
corrections.caveats: Rust library with no C/C++ API, so it is outside the catalog's C/C++ scope. No published numbers against nanoflann or any C++ library: the comparison repo tests only Rust and Python libraries. The Kiddo repo does have an FFI harness for nanoflann, ALGLIB and Pkd-tree (benches/profile_cpp_competitors.rs, charted by scripts/chart_cpp_competitor_results.py), but no results were found on any reachable page; the results site sdd.github.io is blocked. Parallel against serial: the Kiddo, nabo and FNNTW benches run the 1,000 queries per iteration with rayon par_iter on a 12-core/24-thread CPU, while scipy's KDTree.query is called with the default workers=1 (the bench comments 'workers=-1 makes this slower?') and sklearn's is single-threaded, so the 18-38x over scipy and sklearn mostly measures threading. pykdtree (a C extension) may use OpenMP, so it is the closest like-for-like competitor (about 1.5-3x on queries, slower on construction). At 1,000 queries per iteration (about 50-80 microseconds), rayon dispatch and Python call overheads are a sizeable share of each sample. Published numbers cover Kiddo v1-v5 (last updated 2024-12-04); the current release is v6.3.0. The README says the data lie on a unit sphere but the bench code uses uniform cube data. The author benchmarks his own library (disclosed). all-benchmarks.json has duplicate 'Query within radius' rows for Kiddo_v1 and Kiddo_v2 with different values. kd-tree-comparison's Cargo.toml builds kiddo_v5 with the nightly-only 'simd' feature.

Shortcoming worth recording: the headline scipy/sklearn gaps compare rayon-parallel queries against single-threaded queries.
